name: Git & GitHub
description: The object model, branching, merge vs rebase, recovery from mistakes and collaborating through pull requests.

modules.name: The Object Model
modules.description: What git actually stores, and why that makes the commands make sense.

cards.prompt: What are git's four object types?
cards.answer: Blob (file contents), tree (a directory listing of blobs and trees), commit (a tree plus parents, author and message) and tag (an annotated pointer). Every object is addressed by the hash of its content.
cards.explanation: A commit is a snapshot, not a diff — diffs are computed on demand. Branches are just files containing a commit hash, which is why creating one is instant. Content addressing is why identical files are stored once and why history cannot be altered silently.

cards.prompt: What are the working tree, the index and HEAD?
cards.answer: The working tree is your files on disk. The index (staging area) is the proposed next commit. HEAD points at the current branch, which points at the last commit.
cards.explanation: Every command is a move between these three: `add` working tree → index, `commit` index → HEAD, `checkout`/`restore` HEAD → working tree. `reset --soft/--mixed/--hard` chooses how far back that move goes.

cards.prompt: Merge vs rebase
cards.answer: Merge records that two lines of work joined, creating a merge commit. Rebase replays your commits on top of the new base, producing a linear history with new commit hashes.

left.title: Merge
points: Busy graph with many merge commits

right.title: Rebase
points: Never rebase a branch others have pulled

cards.explanation: The common convention: rebase your local feature branch onto main to stay current, then merge into main. The golden rule is do not rewrite published history — anyone who pulled it now has a divergent copy.

cards.prompt: What is the difference between these three commands?
cards.code:
git reset --soft  HEAD~1
git reset --mixed HEAD~1   # default
git reset --hard  HEAD~1
cards.answer: `--soft` moves HEAD back but keeps changes staged. `--mixed` moves HEAD and unstages them, leaving files edited. `--hard` moves HEAD and discards the changes entirely.
cards.explanation: Only `--hard` loses work, and even then committed work is recoverable via `git reflog`. Uncommitted changes destroyed by `--hard` are genuinely gone — which is why `git stash` before an experiment is a cheap habit.

modules.name: Daily Practice & Recovery
modules.description: Branching strategies, pull requests, and getting out of trouble.

cards.prompt: You ran `git reset --hard` and lost three commits. Are they gone?
cards.answer: No. `git reflog` lists every position HEAD has held, including orphaned commits. Find the hash and `git checkout -b recovery <hash>` or `git reset --hard <hash>`.
cards.explanation: Reflog is local, kept about 90 days by default, and covers reset, rebase, checkout, merge and amend. Almost anything committed is recoverable — which is the strongest argument for committing early and often, even messily.

cards.prompt: A bad commit is already pushed to main. Revert or reset?
cards.answer: Revert. `git revert <hash>` creates a new commit undoing the change, leaving history intact for everyone. Reset rewrites history and requires a force push that breaks every other clone.
cards.explanation: Rule of thumb: reset for local, unpublished work; revert for anything shared. If you must force-push a shared branch, use `--force-with-lease` so you cannot clobber someone else's commits you have not seen.

cards.prompt: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 400 commits. How do you find which one introduced it?
cards.answer: `git bisect`: mark a known-good and a known-bad commit and git binary-searches between them — about 9 checkouts for 400 commits. With `git bisect run <script>` it is fully automatic.
cards.explanation: This is binary search applied to history, and it is close to magic when a regression has no obvious cause. It rewards small, atomic commits that each build and pass tests — a large commit only narrows the search to itself.

cards.prompt: Trunk-based development vs GitFlow
cards.answer: Trunk-based: short-lived branches merged to main daily, releases from main with feature flags. GitFlow: long-lived develop, release and hotfix branches with formal promotion.

left.title: Trunk-based
points: Needs feature flags and strong CI

cards.explanation: Long-lived branches are where merge pain lives: the longer a branch runs, the worse the conflict. Most web teams should default to trunk-based; GitFlow makes more sense when you genuinely maintain several released versions.

cards.prompt: What makes a good commit message?
cards.answer: A short imperative subject (~50 chars) saying what the commit does, a blank line, then a body explaining *why* — the context, the alternatives considered, and any consequence a future reader needs.
cards.explanation: The diff already shows what changed; the message must carry the reasoning, because that is what `git blame` cannot reconstruct. Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`) add machine-readable structure for changelogs and version bumps.

cards.prompt: What makes a pull request easy to review?
cards.answer: One logical change, small enough to read in fifteen minutes, a description covering what and why, green CI, self-review comments on anything non-obvious, and no unrelated formatting churn.
cards.explanation: Review quality collapses with size — beyond a few hundred lines people skim and approve. Split refactors from behaviour changes into separate commits or PRs so the reviewer can see the real change instead of hunting it inside a reformat.

modules.name: Everyday Power Tools
modules.description: Fetch versus pull, stash, cherry-pick, interactive rebase, conflicts, tags, detached HEAD and the modern switch/restore commands.

cards.prompt: `git fetch` vs `git pull`
cards.answer: `fetch` downloads new commits and updates remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`) without touching your work; `pull` is `fetch` followed by integrating the upstream branch into your current branch — a merge by default, or a rebase with `--rebase`.

right.title: pull
points: Can create merge commits or conflicts

cards.explanation: Fetching first lets you inspect what changed (`git log HEAD..origin/main`) before integrating. Setting `pull.rebase=true` (or `pull.ff=only`) avoids a stream of pointless "Merge branch main" commits on feature branches.

cards.prompt: What does `git stash` do, and what are its pitfalls?
cards.answer: It shelves uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) onto a stack and resets the working tree, so you can switch context; `git stash pop` reapplies the latest and drops it, `apply` keeps it. `-u` includes untracked files.
cards.explanation: Stashes are easy to forget and are not tied to a branch — old ones pile up in `git stash list`. For anything longer than a quick switch, a WIP commit on a branch (amended later) or a separate worktree (`git worktree add`) is safer and more visible.

cards.prompt: What does `git cherry-pick` do, and when is it the right tool?
cards.answer: It applies the changes introduced by specific existing commits onto the current branch as new commits (with new hashes). Typical use: backporting a fix from main to a release branch.
cards.explanation: Frequent cherry-picking between long-lived branches duplicates commits and invites confusing conflicts later, so treat it as a surgical tool. `-x` records the original commit hash in the message, which keeps backports traceable.

cards.prompt: What can `git rebase -i` do to a branch's history?
cards.answer: Reorder commits, squash or fixup several into one, reword messages, edit a commit's contents, split a commit, or drop commits — all before the branch is shared. `git commit --fixup=<sha>` plus `rebase -i --autosquash` folds review fixes into the right commit automatically.
cards.explanation: The goal is a history of logical, reviewable, bisectable steps. It rewrites hashes, so only do it on commits nobody else has based work on; push the result with `--force-with-lease`.

cards.prompt: How should you resolve a merge conflict well?
cards.answer: Read both sides and understand the intent of each change (`git log --merge` and `git diff` help), edit to the correct combined result rather than picking a side blindly, remove the markers, run the tests, then `git add` and continue. Enable `merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3` to see the common ancestor.
cards.explanation: Seeing the base version shows what each side actually changed, which makes most conflicts obvious. `git rerere` remembers resolutions for repeated rebases. Frequent integration keeps conflicts small — the real fix is shorter-lived branches.

cards.prompt: Lightweight tags vs annotated tags
cards.answer: A lightweight tag is just a named pointer to a commit; an annotated tag is a full git object with a tagger, date, message and optional signature.

left.title: Lightweight
points: Just a ref to a commit

cards.explanation: Use annotated (and ideally signed) tags for releases — `git describe` and many release tools consider only annotated tags by default. Tags are not pushed with a normal `git push`; use `git push origin v1.2.0` or `--follow-tags`. Never move a published release tag.

cards.prompt: Git says "You are in 'detached HEAD' state". What does that mean, and how do you avoid losing work?
cards.answer: HEAD points directly at a commit instead of at a branch — typically after checking out a tag or a specific hash. You can look around and even commit, but new commits belong to no branch and become unreachable when you switch away. Create a branch to keep them: `git switch -c my-fix`.
cards.explanation: If you already switched away, `git reflog` still lists the orphaned commits for about 90 days, so the work is recoverable. Detached HEAD is also the normal state inside a bisect and in many CI checkouts.

cards.prompt: Why were `git switch` and `git restore` added when `git checkout` already existed?
cards.answer: `checkout` did two unrelated jobs — changing branches and overwriting files — so a typo could silently discard work. `switch` only changes branches (`-c` creates one); `restore` only restores file contents (`--staged` unstages, `--source=<rev>` takes a file from another commit).
cards.explanation: The split makes intent explicit and mistakes rarer. `git restore <file>` discards unstaged changes irreversibly, so use it deliberately; `git restore --staged <file>` is the safe way to unstage.

cards.prompt: What are remotes, remote-tracking branches and upstreams, and how does the fork-and-pull-request flow use them?
cards.answer: A remote is a named URL of another copy of the repository (`origin` by convention). Remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`) record where the remote's branches were at your last fetch. A branch's upstream is the remote branch it pushes to and pulls from, set with `git push -u origin my-branch`.
cards.explanation: In the fork flow, `origin` is your fork and `upstream` is the original project: fetch from upstream to stay current, push branches to origin, and open pull requests from your fork to upstream. `git remote -v` and `git branch -vv` show how everything is wired.

modules.name: Repository Management
modules.description: Ignoring files, hooks, large files, submodules, searching history and signed commits.

cards.prompt: You added `.env` to `.gitignore`, but it still appears in `git status` changes. Why?
cards.answer: `.gitignore` only affects untracked files; `.env` was already committed, so git keeps tracking it. Stop tracking it with `git rm --cached .env`, commit that, and — because it contained secrets and is in history — rotate those secrets.
cards.explanation: Removing it from the latest commit does not remove it from history; it remains in every clone. For secrets that were pushed, rotation is mandatory and history rewriting (`git filter-repo`) is optional cleanup.

cards.prompt: What are git hooks, and why can they not be your only enforcement?
cards.answer: Scripts git runs at points in its workflow — `pre-commit` (lint, format, secret scan), `commit-msg` (message format), `pre-push` (quick tests). Tools such as pre-commit, Husky and lefthook share hook configuration through the repository.
cards.explanation: Hooks run on developers' machines and can be skipped with `--no-verify` or simply not installed, so they are a convenience for fast feedback. The same checks must run in CI, which is the real gate.

cards.prompt: Your repository takes 20 minutes to clone because someone committed video assets and build artefacts. What do you do?
cards.answer: Stop the bleeding: add the paths to `.gitignore` and move large binaries to Git LFS or external artefact storage. The history still contains the blobs, so rewrite it with `git filter-repo` (coordinating a re-clone for everyone) if clone size matters — or use partial and shallow clones as a stop-gap.
cards.explanation: Git stores every version of every file forever, and binary files do not delta-compress well. Build outputs never belong in git; large source assets belong in LFS from the start. `git count-objects -vH` and `git-sizer` show where the size comes from.

cards.prompt: Git submodules vs a package manager dependency
cards.answer: A submodule embeds another repository at a pinned commit inside yours; a package-manager dependency pulls a versioned release from a registry.

left.title: Submodule
points: Extra commands and easy to desync

right.title: Package dependency
points: Resolved and locked by the tool

cards.explanation: Submodules need `--recurse-submodules` on clone and update, and are easy to leave out of sync, which confuses newcomers. Prefer published packages for dependencies; use submodules only when you genuinely need another repository's source at a fixed commit and no package exists.

cards.prompt: How do you find when a specific line or function changed, or when a string was introduced?
cards.answer: `git log -S "text"` (the pickaxe) finds commits that added or removed that string; `-G regex` matches changed lines; `git log -L :funcName:file` shows the history of one function; `git blame -w -C` attributes lines while ignoring whitespace and following moves.
cards.explanation: Add large formatting commits to a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file so `blame` skips them. Combined with good commit messages, these commands answer "why is this code like this?" — often faster than asking anyone.

cards.prompt: What does commit signing prove, and why does the author field alone prove nothing?
cards.answer: Anyone can set any name and email in `user.name` and `user.email`, so the author field is a claim. A signature made with the committer's GPG or SSH key proves the commit came from the holder of that key, which hosting platforms show as "Verified".
cards.explanation: Branch protection can require signed commits. Signing with SSH keys (`gpg.format=ssh`) reuses keys developers already have. It is one link in supply-chain integrity alongside protected branches, reviews and signed release artefacts.
